title: Europe Can’t Appease Protesters Anymore
author: Dario Marino
content:
![Europe Can’t Appease Protesters
Anymore](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/10/AP26290687287089.jpg)

After the Second World War, Europe sought to build a new social order that
would mark a dramatic break with its recent militaristic and undemocratic
past. One of the elements of this order was that the masses would be able to
protest with state protection. The consensus was that this would strengthen
the democratic spirit, allowing political contestation to happen not only in
parliament, but in the streets.

The latest wave of protests is testing what remains of this consensus. On
October 17, around 550,000 people [_protested across
France_](https://www.reuters.com/world/students-trade-unions-yellow-vests-set-
protest-across-france-2026-10-17/?ref=compactmag.com), and masked arsonists
[_burned down_](https://www.reuters.com/world/frances-limoges-fire-ravaged-
town-hall-rekindles-memories-notre-dame-2026-10-18/?ref=compactmag.com) the
town hall of Limoges and [_set Lyon 's tourism office on
fire._](https://www.bbc.com/news/videos/ck20wn97e96yo?ref=compactmag.com) The
violent protests have also [_expanded to
Italy_](https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c6j9kwxxmxydo?ref=compactmag.com),
and the largest union in Italy, CGIL, called for a [_national
strike_](https://www.dw.com/en/meloni-backs-police-after-cost-of-living-
protests-turn-violent-in-italian-cities/a-79692755?ref=compactmag.com).

Appeasement has long been European governments' preferred response to such
episodes. In [_Italy_](https://www.britannica.com/topic/Statute-of-the-
Workers?ref=compactmag.com) and
[_France_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labor_Code_\(France\)?ref=compactmag.com)
in the 1970s, major concessions to organized labor consolidated its power.
More recently in France, the [__Gilet Jaunes_
protests_](https://www.npr.org/2018/12/10/675382720/french-president-macron-
makes-concessions-to-yellow-vest-protesters?ref=compactmag.com) led the
government to walk back the proposed carbon tax, and the [_pension reform
protests_](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2025/10/14/french-prime-minister-
backs-suspending-unpopular-pension-reform-law?ref=compactmag.com) led to the
suspension of Emmanuel Macron's plan to raise the retirement age from sixty-
two to sixty-four.
